messages.subject: Re: Estimated D less than naïve
parts:
Thanks for the vote of confidence Alex.

Related to your walking transects twice; you have not increased the=20
number of transects, just the amount of effort you exerted on those=20
transects. You still have only 6 transects, so that is the number of=20
records that your Distance project will have in the 'Line Transect'=20
layer. That is the number of replicates that will be used to estimate=20
the encounter rate variance. However, by walking them twice you will=20
have increased the number of detections you have for fitting your=20
detection function.

You supply Distance with the information about the fact that you walked=20
the transects twice by doubling the length of the transects in the 'Line=20
length' field of the 'Line Transect' layer. This will keep the=20
calculations correct (walking twice as far and seeing twice as many=20
possums will result in the same encounter rate: you're doubling both=20
numerator and denominator). But to stay out of 'pseudoreplication jail'=20
keep the number of transects set at 6.

Alex Diment wrote:
> > Hi Eric,
> >
> > Yes, your guesses are pretty close!
> >
> > The ESW is 17m, though the area is rectangular (L=3D2457), and the poin=
t estimate of N is actually 28, so that probably accounts for you being a=
wee bit off.
> >
> > I'm amazed that the maths copes seamlessly with this sort of double cou=
nting! I remember you telling us that, and I told the possum-hunters not =
to worry if it's the same animal, but I still can't quite work out how it=
"knows" - it's clearly very clever!
> >
> >
> > On a slightly different issue, how do I cope with repeated counts. In =
another area, they only had 6 transects, so repeated them the next night =
to bump up the number of transects. How can I handle this without doing =
any naughty pseudoreplication?
> >
> >
> > I'll be back in the UK from next year, so will try very hard to come fo=
r a refresher course at St Andrews.
> > Thanks heaps for your insights!
> >
> > Best,
> > Alex.
> >
> > Alex Diment
> > Institute of Wildlife Research
> > University of Sydney
> >
> > -----Original Message-----
> > From: Eric Rexstad [mailto:er...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk]=20
> > Sent: Wednesday, August 26, 2009 9:31 PM
> > To: Alex Diment
> > Cc: DISTANCE...@jiscmail.ac.uk
> > Subject: Re: [DIST-SAMP] Estimated D less than na=EFve estimate
> >
> > Alex:
> >
> > There's not quite enough information in your question to find the solut=
ion, but I've followed this logic to think about your problem:
> >
> > If your study area is 5.3ha, I'll pretend it is square, so that would m=
ake it 230m on a side. If you placed 9 transects into that site, I'll pr=
etend that you placed them systematically running north-to-south. If the=
y are equally spaced, then they will need to be spaced roughly 29m apart =
(9 transects have 8 spaces between them; 8 goes into 230 28.75 times).
> >
> > I'm using the density estimation approach that uses effective strip hal=
f-width (ESW, or mu); this is eqn 1.3 on p.5 of Buckland et al.=20
> > (2001). D=3Dn/(2.mu.L)
> >
> > From the information you provided, n=3D44, L=3D2250m, and A=3D5.3ha. =
It is information about the detection function that lets us estimate mu, =
so I'm going to guess about mu. If I guess that mu=3D10m (meaning that y=
ou effectively see as many possums at perpendicular distances beyond 100m=
as you missed at distances less than mu), then I get a density estimate =
of 44/(2.10m.2250m)=3D44/45,000m^2. Converting m^2 to ha, we get 44anima=
ls in 4.5ha or about 10 animal per hectare (within the covered region of =
your sampling). Scaling that up to the 5.3ha study area, we estimate the=
number of animals to be 10 x 5.3 or 53 animals in the study area.
> >
> > The bigger the estimate of mu, the smaller the estimate of density. So=
, you'll get your estimate of abundance (25) if your estimated effective =
strip half-width is about 20.7m. Was that your estimate of ESW (shown in=
your Distance output)?
> >
> > This brings me back to my guess about your design. If your transects w=
ere placed something like 29m apart, and the estimated strip half-width w=
as 20.7m, then the area effectively sampled by your consecutive transects=
would overlap (20.7m to the right of the left transect and 20.7m to the =
left of the right transect being greater than the inter-transect separati=
on). That suggests that the covered region (the area your sampling cover=
ed) exceeded the size of the study area. This can result in the paradox =
you observed in your analysis.
> >
> > How many of my guesses were incorrect?
> >
> > Alex Diment wrote:
> > =20
>> >> Hi,
>> >>
>> >> I'm probably doing something really wrong, and it's been way too long =
since the Workshop in Perth, but I've got an issue which I can't understa=
nd.
>> >>
>> >> I've got data from a survey of a 5.3ha site, where 44 possums were obs=
erved over 9 transects (each about 250m long).
>> >>
>> >> The distance data seem reasonably well behaved, and I've fitted a few =
models which look OK, but they give me estimates of D of about 5, (theref=
ore N about 25) which is weird, since 44 possums were seen!
>> >>
>> >> Am I being stupid? I can't see any obvious errors, in the units or an=
ything...
>> >>
